newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq said to cooperate with U.N. on weapons.
newsitem.headline: Iraq said to cooperate with U.N. on weapons.

text.p: Iraq has responded in writing to United Nations concerns about its weapons programmes in hopes of having curbs on its oil exports completely removed by the end of this year, U.N. and diplomatic sources in Baghdad have said.
They said the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) was encouraged by the cooperation and would send chemical experts to Iraq on March 27 for a seminar with Iraqi chemical warfare specialists.
Iraq is compelled under the 1991 Gulf War ceasefire terms to rid itself of weapons of mass destruction and the means to produce them. UNSCOM is responsible for overseeing this.

The talks, the first of their kind since the United Nations started its disarmament activities in Iraq in April 1991 after the Gulf War, will take place before UNSCOM's chairman Rolf Ekeus comes to Baghdad in the first week of April.
The Iraqis, the sources said, were eager to make as much progress as possible on remaining issues before Ekeus presents his next report to the U.N. Security Council on April 11.
One diplomat said the two sides, after bitter recriminations, were now focusing on long-range missiles and chemical arms.
"I think the biological warfare file is more complicated and may need some more time," the diplomat said.

UNSCOM last month transferred more than 100 pieces of wreckage from long-range missiles to the United States to see whether they were locally produced or authentic parts of Scuds that Iraq bought from the former Soviet Union.

"The government of Iraq has started answering our concerns particularly on missiles and chemical arms in writing...Experts from both sides will soon meet in a seminar...It is too early to say what will happen but the next few weeks are important," Roger Knight, deputy director of Baghdad's Ongoing Monitoring and Verification Centre, told Reuters last week.
Knight said the written replies were on issues Ekeus had raised during his latest Baghdad trip in February.
"Of course we need to verify any written Iraqi declaration. We also need to interview Iraqi scientists involved in past programmes," he said.
Ekeus has said his commission could finish its disarmament activities in Iraq in six months if the Baghdad government fully cooperated with his weapons inspectors.
"Maybe that is what the Iraqis have in mind. Past experience is full of ups and downs in cooperation. Let us wait and see," said another diplomat.
One diplomat said Iraq's rush to full cooperation with UNSCOM could be because of dissatisfaction with the way its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations was working.

The agreement, implemented in December, allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months in return for food and medicine to alleviate hardship caused by U.N. sanctions imposed after its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Little food or medicine from the deal has yet been handed out to the Iraqis.

"Weighing pros and cons, the Iraqis may have come to the conclusion that heeding Ekeus's demands, even if outside the scope of U.N. resolutions in their opinion, will bring more fruits than the oil deal," the diplomat said.
The current partial exports as well as the purchase of food and medicine along with their distribution have to be carried out under strict U.N. monitoring.

Iraq's envoy Abdul-Amir al-Anbari, who negotiated the oil deal with the United Nations, said on Friday he believed Iraq would be able to satisfy Ekeus by the end of 1997 and resume free oil exports by then.
